script.opening: "Hi, I'm really sorry to call, I'm probably overreacting — my little girl Lily, she's seven weeks old, she feels hot and I took her temperature and it's 38.2. She's a bit more sleepy than usual and not feeding as well today. Can I just give her some Calpol and keep an eye on her at home? I don't want to drag a newborn to hospital if it's just a cold."

facts.text: Measured with a digital under-arm thermometer 20 minutes ago: 38.2°C. Rechecked: 38.3°C. You have not given any Calpol yet.
Breastfed. Normally feeds every 3 hours for 20 minutes; today feeds are short and she falls asleep after five minutes. Two wet nappies since this morning (usually five or six by now).
Sleepier than usual and harder to rouse for feeds, but she does wake and cries when changed. Cry is normal, not high-pitched. Colour a little pale; hands and feet cool. No blue lips.
Breathing "a bit fast" when you watch her chest; no grunting, no pauses, no sucking in under the ribs that you can see.
No rash. If asked to check the soft spot: "It feels normal, not bulging." No vomiting, no diarrhoea, no fits, no stiffness or floppiness. Your partner has had a cold this week.
Born at 39 weeks, normal delivery, no problems; went home after a day. Mum did not have a fever in labour as far as you know. No medicines. 8-week vaccines not given yet.
You are Jess, 28; Lily is your first baby. Partner at work; your mum lives 10 minutes away and could drive. Car seat available.

Apologetic and hoping for "Calpol and see". If the doctor explains that babies under three months with a temperature need to be checked in hospital today, you are frightened: "Is it something serious?" If they explain calmly and give clear instructions, agree to go now. Ask: "Should I give her Calpol first?"

ice.ideas: "It's probably just the cold her dad's got."
ice.concerns: "I don't want to be the overreacting mum" — but you are worried by how sleepy she is.
ice.expectations: "Can I just give Calpol and keep an eye?" You will go straight to hospital if it is explained clearly.

cues: "I'm probably overreacting." — say in the opening.
"She's more sleepy than usual." — say in the opening.
"Only two wet nappies today." — say if asked about nappies.

checkpoints.text: Recognises that a temperature ≥38°C in an infant UNDER 3 MONTHS is a NICE NG143 RED flag mandating URGENT face-to-face assessment — and does NOT advise home management with Calpol "and keep an eye"

Weights the additional concerning features (more sleepy, feeding less) and screens/asks about colour, responsiveness, breathing, hydration (wet nappies) and rash — while recognising the age + fever alone already triggers urgent assessment

Arranges URGENT assessment NOW: same-day paediatric/emergency assessment (the infant needs to be SEEN, typically with septic-screen evaluation in secondary care) — not a routine GP appointment or telephone reassurance
Conveys that antipyretics do NOT make a febrile young infant safe and that the age + fever is the trigger regardless of how she looks between feeds — so this is not deferrable
Gives clear, practical instructions to get her seen (where to go / arranging it) and the threshold for 999 (worsening, non-blanching rash, breathing difficulty, unresponsiveness, fits, mottled/pale)
VALIDATES the mother’s instinct and explicitly counters the "overreacting/don’t want to be a nuisance" minimisation — she did exactly the right thing — while not inducing paralysing panic
Communicates the urgency calmly and supportively, giving concrete doable actions so she accepts and acts on the need for assessment

Safety-nets unambiguously: urgent assessment today, what to watch en route, 999 criteria (non-blanching rash, breathing trouble, unresponsiveness, mottling/seizure), and ensures she will go — not Calpol-and-wait for a febrile 7-week-old

worked.txt: "First — you are absolutely NOT overreacting, and you did exactly the right thing ringing. Here’s the important rule: a temperature of 38 or more in a baby under three months old is something we always get seen straightaway, today, in person. Babies this tiny can get unwell quickly and don’t always show it, so we don’t manage a fever at this age at home."

"I know the instinct is Calpol and watch — but at seven weeks, a fever isn’t something to treat at home and keep an eye on. The Calpol would just lower the number; it wouldn’t make her safe. The fact that she’s seven weeks AND has a fever is the reason she needs to be looked at properly, whatever she’s like between feeds."

"And you’ve noticed she’s more sleepy and not feeding as well — that’s exactly the kind of thing that adds to my wanting her seen quickly. You know her best, and your gut that something’s off is worth trusting."

"So this is what I’d like you to do: take her to be assessed now — I’ll arrange where, the paediatric/children’s assessment, today. They’ll check her over properly and do some tests to be sure there’s no infection brewing. This isn’t me frightening you; it’s just how we look after babies this small with a fever."

"While you’re getting ready or on the way — if she becomes harder to wake, her breathing looks fast or laboured, she goes pale/mottled or blue, has a fit, or you see any rash that doesn’t fade when you press a glass on it — call 999 immediately, don’t wait. Is there someone who can go with you?"

"You haven’t made a fuss — you’ve done the textbook right thing. Most of the time these little ones are fine, but the only safe way to know with a fever this young is to have her checked. Go now, and they’ll take it from there. You’re a good mum trusting your instincts."

f.learning: A temperature of 38°C or above in an infant UNDER 3 MONTHS is a NICE NG143 traffic-light RED feature in its own right — because young infants are at high risk of serious bacterial infection/sepsis and can deteriorate rapidly with few localising signs — so it mandates URGENT face-to-face assessment (paediatric/emergency) today, NOT home management with antipyretics. Antipyretics treat the number, not the cause, and do not make a febrile young infant safe; the age + fever is the trigger regardless of how the baby looks between feeds, and here the added features (more sleepy, feeding less) heighten concern. The examinable hidden agenda is a first-time mum minimising ("probably overreacting", "don’t want to drag a newborn to hospital") out of not wanting to be a nuisance while quietly terrified — validate her instinct explicitly (she did exactly the right thing), be unambiguous that this must be seen urgently, convey it calmly without paralysing panic, arrange the assessment now, and safety-net the 999 criteria (non-blanching rash, breathing difficulty, unresponsiveness, mottling, seizure).

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG143 — Fever in under 5s (2019) · NICE NG254 — Suspected sepsis in under 16s (2025) · NICE NG224 — Urinary tract infection in under 16s (2022) · BNFC
knowledge.summary: A temperature of 38°C or more in a baby under 3 months is a NICE NG143 red feature on its own. Lily needs urgent face-to-face paediatric assessment today, not paracetamol and watching at home.

points.t: NICE NG143: temperature ≥38°C in an infant under 3 months is a red (high-risk) feature. Young infants can have serious bacterial infection with few signs, and a well-looking baby does not exclude it.

NICE NG143: a child with any red feature who is not in immediate danger should be assessed face to face within 2 hours; an immediately life-threatening picture needs an emergency ambulance. In practice a febrile infant under 3 months goes straight to the paediatric team.

Colour (pale, mottled, blue), activity (hard to wake, weak or high-pitched cry, not responding normally), breathing (fast, grunting, recession), hydration (reduced feeds, fewer wet nappies) and a non-blanching rash. Reduced feeding and sleepiness add to the concern.

NICE NG143 for infants under 3 months with fever: observations, FBC, CRP, blood culture and urine testing, with lumbar puncture and parenteral antibiotics depending on age, how unwell the baby looks and the white cell count. A febrile infant under 3 months with possible UTI is referred immediately to paediatric specialist care (NICE NG224).

NICE NG143: don’t use antipyretics with the sole aim of reducing body temperature, and don’t rely on a fall or lack of fall in temperature at 1 to 2 hours to judge whether illness is serious; paracetamol or ibuprofen can be considered for a febrile child who appears distressed. Paracetamol for an infant this young only per BNFC and the assessing clinician.
Assess for sepsis using NICE NG254 in under 16s. A parent’s concern that the baby is not themselves is itself an important warning sign.

After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.

model.text: Hello, it’s Dr Adeyemi from the surgery. You’re calling about Lily — can you confirm her date of birth, and that you’re her mum?
model.why: Confirms identity and parental responsibility by phone

model.text: Yes, I’m her mum. Sorry, I’m probably overreacting. She’s seven weeks, she feels hot and her temperature is 38.2. She’s sleepier than usual and not feeding as well. Can I just give her Calpol and keep an eye on her?
You are not overreacting — ringing was exactly the right thing to do. I need to ask a few quick questions and then I’ll tell you clearly what we need to do. Is Lily with you now?
model.why: Validates her instinct immediately and sets a short, clear agenda

model.text: Yes, she’s in my arms.
How did you take her temperature, and when?
With our thermometer, just before I rang.
Thank you. Looking at her now: is she waking up and looking at you, or is she hard to rouse?
model.why: Assesses responsiveness, a key red feature

model.text: She opens her eyes, but she’s dozier than normal.
What’s her colour like — pink as usual, or pale, blotchy or bluish? And her breathing — fast, noisy, or can you see her tummy or ribs pulling in?
model.why: Screens colour and respiratory red features

model.text: I haven’t noticed anything like that. I don’t really know what I’m looking for.
That’s fine — that’s what we’re here for. How many wet nappies today, and has she been sick at all?
I haven’t been counting. I’m not sure.
And any rash anywhere, especially spots that don’t fade when pressed?
I haven’t seen one.
You said you don’t want to drag her to hospital if it’s just a cold. What’s worrying you most right now?
model.why: Surfaces the fear under the minimisation

model.text: That something’s really wrong and I won’t know. She’s so tiny. But I don’t want to waste anyone’s time.

You’re not wasting anyone’s time. Here’s the important rule: any baby under three months with a temperature of 38 or more needs to be seen in person today by the children’s team. Babies this young can have an infection without showing many signs, so we never manage a fever at this age at home.
model.why: States the NG143 red-flag rule clearly and without ambiguity

model.text: Even if she seems okay between feeds?

Even then. Calpol would bring the number down, but it wouldn’t tell us what’s causing it or make her safe. Her age and the temperature together are the reason — and you’ve also noticed she’s sleepier and feeding less, which makes me want her seen quickly.
model.why: Explains why antipyretics and watchful waiting are unsafe here

model.text: Okay. That’s frightening.

I understand. Most babies who are checked turn out to have something minor, but the only safe way to know is for the team to examine her and do some tests, usually a urine test and blood tests. You’re doing exactly what a good mum does.
model.why: Acknowledges fear and gives honest, proportionate reassurance

model.text: So here’s the plan. I’m going to ring the children’s assessment unit now so they’re expecting Lily, and I need you to take her there straight away. Can you get there now, and is anyone able to come with you?
model.why: Arranges urgent assessment and checks practical barriers

model.text: I can get there. I’ll see who can come with me.
Good. Bring her red book and a feed. Keep her in light clothes — don’t wrap her up tightly. If there’s any problem getting there quickly, call 999 rather than waiting.
model.why: Practical, doable instructions and a fallback

model.text: Okay.

On the way, call 999 straight away if she becomes hard to wake, her breathing looks fast or she’s struggling, she goes pale, blotchy or blue, she has a fit, or you see a rash that doesn’t fade under a glass. Can you tell me back what you’re going to do?
Go to the children’s unit now. If she’s hard to wake, struggling to breathe, goes blue or blotchy, has a fit or a rash that doesn’t fade, I ring 999.
Exactly. I’m calling them as soon as we hang up, and I’ll check in with the team later today. You trusted your instinct, and that’s the most important thing you could have done for her.
model.why: Confirms handover and follow-up, and closes by affirming the parent

model.text: Thank you. We’re going now.

social.t: Fear of being seen as over-anxious leads parents to minimise. Say explicitly that calling was right, so she calls again next time.
Transport, other children and being alone with a sick baby delay attendance. Ask, and give 999 as the fallback.

legal.t: Confirm you are speaking to someone with parental responsibility. Decisions about Lily’s care are made with her parent in Lily’s best interests.

professional.t: Telephone assessment cannot exclude serious illness in a young infant. Document the red feature, the advice given, the handover to paediatrics and the safety-net (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Phone ahead to the paediatric team and check later that she arrived. A referral nobody acts on is not a safe plan.

community.t: Health visitor for support after discharge. Parent information on spotting a seriously ill child from NHS sources and the paediatric team.

redFlags: Age under 3 months with temperature ≥38°C — red on its own (NICE NG143)
Hard to rouse, weak or high-pitched cry, pale/mottled/blue, grunting or fast breathing
Non-blanching rash, seizure, reduced wet nappies or poor feeding
psychosocial: First-time mother minimising to avoid being a nuisance
Who can go with her, and how she will get there
ice: Concern: something serious being missed in a tiny baby
Expectation: permission to give Calpol and watch at home

playbook.diagnosis: Be unambiguous: “Any baby under three months with a temperature of 38 or more needs to be seen in person today. That’s the rule, and it applies to Lily whatever she seems like between feeds.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “A tiny baby’s body is like a smoke alarm that doesn’t go off until the fire is big. The temperature is the only early warning we get, so we act on it straight away.”

management.reflectIce: “You said you’re probably overreacting. You’re not — you noticed she wasn’t herself and you rang. That’s exactly what she needed you to do.”
management.psychosocial: Solve getting there: someone to go with her, the red book and a feed, and 999 if transport is a problem or she worsens.
sharedPlan: Urgent same-day face-to-face paediatric assessment — phone ahead
safetyNet: 999 if hard to wake, breathing difficulty, pale/mottled/blue, seizure or non-blanching rash
GP to check with the paediatric team later that day

pitfalls.intro: This station has one non-negotiable: a febrile baby under 3 months is seen today. Candidates fail by being talked down by a calm parent, or by getting the rule right but frightening the mother so much that she can’t take in the plan.

items.fail: Agreeing to Calpol and a call back if she worsens.
items.why: “Unsafe management.” NICE NG143 makes fever under 3 months a red feature on its own.
items.fix: State the rule in the first half of the call and don’t negotiate on it.

items.fail: Being reassured because the baby “seems okay between feeds”.
items.why: Young infants can have serious infection with few signs; appearance on the phone is unreliable.
items.fix: “Even if she seems okay, her age and the temperature are the reason she needs to be seen.”

items.fail: Spending most of the call on a detailed history.
items.why: The decision is already made at the opening sentence. Time spent after that delays the baby.
items.fix: A two-minute traffic-light screen, then act.

items.fail: Telling her it could be meningitis or sepsis without context.
items.why: “Did not respond to the patient’s concerns.” Panic can stop a parent taking in the practical steps.
items.fix: Calm and honest: “Most babies turn out fine, but this is how we keep babies this small safe.”

items.fail: Saying “go to A&E” and ending the call.
items.why: “Follow-up not arranged.” No handover, no check she can get there, no 999 criteria.
items.fix: Phone ahead, ask about transport and a companion, give specific 999 triggers, use teach-back.

items.fail: Letting “sorry, I’m probably overreacting” pass without comment.
items.why: Parents who feel foolish delay calling next time.
items.fix: “You’re not overreacting — ringing was exactly right.” Say it early and again at the close.

Serious bacterial infection including sepsis, meningitis and UTI vs a viral illness — not distinguishable by phone.
Screened responsiveness, colour, breathing, hydration and non-blanching rash; recognised age plus fever as red regardless.
Stated clearly that a fever at 7 weeks is a red flag needing assessment today.
Did not advise Calpol-and-wait; phoned ahead to paediatrics; practical instructions for getting there.
Addressed transport, a companion, feeding and clothing on the way.
Explicit 999 criteria, teach-back, handover to the paediatric team and a check later that day.

social.t: Fear of being seen as over-anxious leads parents to minimise. Say explicitly that calling was right, so she calls again next time.
Transport, other children and being alone with a sick baby delay attendance. Ask, and give 999 as the fallback.

legal.t: Confirm you are speaking to someone with parental responsibility. Decisions about Lily’s care are made with her parent in Lily’s best interests.

professional.t: Telephone assessment cannot exclude serious illness in a young infant. Document the red feature, the advice given, the handover to paediatrics and the safety-net (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Phone ahead to the paediatric team and check later that she arrived. A referral nobody acts on is not a safe plan.

community.t: Health visitor for support after discharge. Parent information on spotting a seriously ill child from NHS sources and the paediatric team.

redFlags: Age under 3 months with temperature ≥38°C — red on its own (NICE NG143)
Hard to rouse, weak or high-pitched cry, pale/mottled/blue, grunting or fast breathing
Non-blanching rash, seizure, reduced wet nappies or poor feeding
psychosocial: First-time mother minimising to avoid being a nuisance
Who can go with her, and how she will get there
ice: Concern: something serious being missed in a tiny baby
Expectation: permission to give Calpol and watch at home

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be unambiguous: “Any baby under three months with a temperature of 38 or more needs to be seen in person today. That’s the rule, and it applies to Lily whatever she seems like between feeds.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “A tiny baby’s body is like a smoke alarm that doesn’t go off until the fire is big. The temperature is the only early warning we get, so we act on it straight away.”

management.reflectIce: “You said you’re probably overreacting. You’re not — you noticed she wasn’t herself and you rang. That’s exactly what she needed you to do.”
management.psychosocial: Solve getting there: someone to go with her, the red book and a feed, and 999 if transport is a problem or she worsens.
sharedPlan: Urgent same-day face-to-face paediatric assessment — phone ahead
safetyNet: 999 if hard to wake, breathing difficulty, pale/mottled/blue, seizure or non-blanching rash
GP to check with the paediatric team later that day

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station has one non-negotiable: a febrile baby under 3 months is seen today. Candidates fail by being talked down by a calm parent, or by getting the rule right but frightening the mother so much that she can’t take in the plan.

items.fail: Agreeing to Calpol and a call back if she worsens.
items.why: “Unsafe management.” NICE NG143 makes fever under 3 months a red feature on its own.
items.fix: State the rule in the first half of the call and don’t negotiate on it.

items.fail: Being reassured because the baby “seems okay between feeds”.
items.why: Young infants can have serious infection with few signs; appearance on the phone is unreliable.
items.fix: “Even if she seems okay, her age and the temperature are the reason she needs to be seen.”

items.fail: Spending most of the call on a detailed history.
items.why: The decision is already made at the opening sentence. Time spent after that delays the baby.
items.fix: A two-minute traffic-light screen, then act.

items.fail: Telling her it could be meningitis or sepsis without context.
items.why: “Did not respond to the patient’s concerns.” Panic can stop a parent taking in the practical steps.
items.fix: Calm and honest: “Most babies turn out fine, but this is how we keep babies this small safe.”

items.fail: Saying “go to A&E” and ending the call.
items.why: “Follow-up not arranged.” No handover, no check she can get there, no 999 criteria.
items.fix: Phone ahead, ask about transport and a companion, give specific 999 triggers, use teach-back.

items.fail: Letting “sorry, I’m probably overreacting” pass without comment.
items.why: Parents who feel foolish delay calling next time.
items.fix: “You’re not overreacting — ringing was exactly right.” Say it early and again at the close.
